tells: Short declarative sentences, Sheikh Bahmanpour named and reported plainly ('Sheikh Bahmanpour says...'), and the quotation 'These are shirk.' is glossed straight after with a plain definition. This matches the reference's way of introducing and then explaining a quotation.

Each quotation is set inside a sentence and then explained in plain words ('What the prayer asks to lose is the heart's love for the world, not the world itself'), and the second paragraph builds on the first ('the same severance from the other side'). Both habits match the reference.
'The reward.' is a verbless fragment used as a signpost inside the prose. Author A always writes full sentences and would fold this in, e.g. 'The first gift is nearness.'
'in the lecturer's reading' is impersonal. Author A always names the speaker ('Sheikh Bahmanpour reads it as...').

'The second gift is a different kind of life.' and 'The third gift is peace.' are teaser lines that close a paragraph by announcing the next one. Author A ends a paragraph on its own point and starts the next point in a new paragraph.
'rise above the concerns that infect everyone else' is coloured, slightly preachy wording. Author A's register is flatter and avoids sweeping lines like 'everyone else'.

'because Islamic mysticism is about something else: catching the signs of Allah: becoming sensitive to them' puts two colons in one sentence on top of a 'because' clause. Author A uses one colon at most and would split this: 'Islamic mysticism is about catching the signs of Allah...'
'and he does not soften it' adds a closing remark about the speaker's attitude to round off the paragraph. Author A ends on the gloss: 'is the gravest charge in Islam.'
'for very different reasons' uses an intensifier Author A avoids; Author A would write 'for different reasons'.
'Sheikh Bahmanpour opened his course by pointing out that' narrates the lecture as an event. Author A states the point and attributes it briefly ('Sheikh Bahmanpour says').

The contrast is balanced with a semicolon, the Sheikh's caveat is reported plainly ('Sheikh Bahmanpour is careful about what this means'), and the paragraph closes on a concrete point rather than a moral, as in the reference.

The chapter opens like the reference's ('These words come near the end of Duʿa Kumayl', 'many of us hear it'), links back to the previous chapter, and states the chapter's subject in one plain line ('This chapter sets out what those prayers ask for').

'ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi's definition says the same thing: "The real gnostic is..."' puts claim, colon and quotation in one sentence and leaves the quotation without comment. Author A sets the quotation inside a sentence ('In Mutahhari's words, the ʿarif "..."') and follows it with a plain gloss.
'Each step of this chapter has led here.' is a signpost about the text itself. Author A moves straight to the point.

'ʿIrfan, then, is worth pursuing: it is the training of the soul...' is a tidy summary line that ends the paragraph with a 'then' wrap-up. Author A ends on a concrete statement (e.g. 'a path that "has a beginning and no end"').
'The only aim worthy of that effort is God Himself.' is grander and more abstract than Author A's register.
Plain, factual short sentences; the quotation is set inside a sentence ('It adds that it is "advisable..."'); and the second paragraph picks up the first ('The other prayers have their own times').

The quotation is placed inside a sentence with 'he writes' and then explained ('He cites them to show...'). The second paragraph picks up the first ('Requests this high raise a difficulty'), echoing the reference's 'Requests like this one'.

The opening links to what came before ('Higher still'), each verse is glossed straight after in plain terms ('Most of us fear Allah's punishment. The people of this verse fear Him...'), and the measured contrast between ordinary believers and those who witness matches the reference.

Quotations are set inside the sentence ('tells the traveller that he "has no right..."', 'It is his own self that he worships, "though..."'), with sober reporting verbs and no editorialising, as in the reference.

The 'If X, then Y' opening picks up the previous step, as in the reference ('If the signs are present and plain...'). After the verse comes a plain reasoning step ('A heart trembles only at the mention of someone it has some experience of'), and the closing line leads into the next verse in the reference's manner.
